title: Build the Pipeline First, Then Fill It With Revenue
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — Email from Joan Braddi to Neal Mohan et al. on Display Strategy
excerptForBlog:
Thanks again for making the time to meet re: our display ads strategy today. A few follow-up notes:

Current State of product strategy (three pillars):

a) Platform to ACCESS the desired inventory. I think we have both the strategy as well as detailed roadmap figured out. We also completed a detailed pricing review and refresh across all products.

b) Ad Exchange to AGGREGATE the inventory that the platform piece gives us access to. Here I think we have the strategy (including positioning to advertisers and publishers) and the roadmap features and timing mostly figured out. One major component we are working on is AdX pricing.

c) Google Content Network to MONETIZE the inventory we aggregate via Ad Exchange and all our AdSense deals. Here we believe that our high level strategy is in place (focus on performance: targeting and optimization) but the roadmap is NOT ready yet. We are working hard on this part and hope to have an initial plan covering the first half of 2009 in place in the next few weeks. It is my highest priority across all the elements of the display strategy.

Based on Omid's feedback, one of the items I am preparing is a quarter-by-quarter review that will include: detailed roadmap for each pillar; our positioning and value proposition to advertisers and publishers; and suggested specific objectives related to display for that quarter.

lessonTitle: Build the Pipeline First, Then Fill It With Revenue
lessonBody:
## 1. Core Message

In September 2008, Google's display ads leadership mapped their strategy as three sequential layers: **access** inventory, **aggregate** it, then **monetize** it. Two of the three layers had clear roadmaps. The third — monetization via the Google Content Network — did not. Braddi says so plainly: "the roadmap is NOT ready yet."

## 2. What the Executive Is Really Thinking

The document reveals a leader doing two things at once. She's reassuring senior leadership that strategy is mostly in hand. But she's also flagging — in writing — that the monetization layer is incomplete, calling it "my highest priority across all the elements of the display strategy." She's not hiding the gap. She's owning it early, before it becomes a fire. The upcoming "quarter-by-quarter review" requested by someone named Omid (context on who this is unclear from the document alone) signals upward accountability pressure and a push for tighter execution tracking.

## 3. Key Management Lessons

### Separate the pipeline from the revenue engine
#### What it means
Braddi's three pillars — access, aggregate, monetize — describe a value chain, not a single product. Each layer must work before the next creates value. You can't monetize inventory you haven't aggregated. You can't aggregate what you can't access.
#### Why it matters
Many companies build revenue features before the underlying infrastructure is solid. The result: leaky growth, poor unit economics, and customer frustration. Getting the sequence right matters as much as building the right things.
#### MBA Perspective
This is **Vertical Integration** logic applied to a platform. Google isn't just building an ad network — it's controlling the entire supply chain from publisher inventory access (AdX) through aggregation to advertiser-facing monetization (Google Content Network). Each layer deepens its control of the market.
#### Real-world application
A SaaS founder building a marketplace should ask: "Do I have the supply side locked in before I chase demand?" Building demand-side features before supply infrastructure is solid is the same mistake Braddi's team is trying to avoid.

### Name the gap out loud
#### What it means
Braddi writes that the monetization roadmap is "NOT ready yet" — in capital letters. She doesn't soften it. She states the problem directly and gives a target: an initial plan covering the first half of 2009, ready "in the next few weeks."
#### Why it matters
Leaders who obscure weak spots from their own teams and executives create delayed problems. The longer a gap stays unnamed, the more expensive it becomes to fix.
#### MBA Perspective
This connects to **Resource-Based View** thinking: you can only allocate resources to a capability gap you've honestly identified. Calling something your "highest priority" without first admitting it's unfinished is meaningless.
#### Real-world application
In your next team review, list the pillars of your strategy and honestly label each one: roadmap clear, roadmap partial, roadmap missing. It's uncomfortable. It's also the only way to fix the right things.

### Strategy and roadmap are not the same thing
#### What it means
Braddi repeatedly distinguishes between having "the strategy" and having "the roadmap." For the monetization pillar, she says the high-level strategy is in place — but the roadmap (specific features, timing, sequencing) is not.
#### Why it matters
This distinction is one of the most commonly collapsed in early-stage companies. Saying "we know we want to monetize through performance advertising" is strategy. Knowing *which* targeting features to ship, in which order, in which quarter — that's a roadmap. One without the other doesn't ship.
#### MBA Perspective
No single named framework required here — this is operational discipline. Strategy sets the direction; roadmap converts direction into decisions.
#### Real-world application
After your next strategy session, ask: "For each goal we just agreed on, do we have a roadmap or just a direction?" If the answer is mostly direction, you're not done.

### Quarterly reviews create accountability gravity
#### What it means
Braddi is preparing a "quarter-by-quarter review" that will track detailed roadmaps, positioning, and specific objectives for each pillar of the display strategy. This wasn't her idea — it came from Omid's feedback.
#### Why it matters
A strategy without a cadence of review drifts. Quarterly checkpoints force teams to commit to concrete milestones rather than vague intentions. They also make gaps visible before they compound.
#### MBA Perspective
This is execution discipline, not a named framework. But the structure — specific objectives, explicit value propositions, time-bound milestones — mirrors the logic of **OKRs** (Objectives and Key Results), though that term doesn't appear in the document.
#### Real-world application
If you have a three-part strategy, build a review document now with one column per pillar and one row per quarter. Leave the incomplete cells blank. The blanks will tell you where to spend your next week.

## 4. Strategic Analysis (MBA Style)

### Competitive Strategy
The three-pillar structure — access, aggregate, monetize — describes a platform strategy designed to sit between publishers and advertisers and capture value at every layer. By controlling both AdX (the supply-side aggregator) and the Google Content Network (the demand-side monetizer), Google is building a structure where competing at any one layer becomes very difficult without competing at all three.

### Risk Analysis
The explicit risk named in the document is execution risk on monetization. The roadmap for the Google Content Network is incomplete, and Braddi says so. The implicit risk: if monetization lags, the access and aggregation layers generate infrastructure costs without proportional revenue return. The strategy also implies pricing risk — "AdX pricing" is flagged as a major open component for the aggregation pillar.

### Build vs Buy Analysis
The document describes a build strategy — internal roadmaps, internal product development across all three pillars. It does not reference any acquisition. Context note: the document is dated September 2008, and the surrounding competitive landscape (including DoubleClick, which Google had acquired) is not discussed in this document, so no claim can be made about prior M&A decisions from this source alone.

### Market Dynamics
The structure of the strategy — controlling access to publisher inventory, aggregating it in an exchange, then monetizing it through a demand-side network — suggests a market where fragmentation is the problem being solved. Publishers have inventory; advertisers want reach; the exchange is the connective tissue. Whoever owns the exchange sets the rules.

### Long-Term Strategic Implications
If all three pillars execute well and connect cleanly, the result is a closed loop: Google controls how inventory is accessed, how it's priced in the exchange, and how advertisers buy it. Each layer creates data that improves the others. If the monetization roadmap stays incomplete, the loop doesn't close and the infrastructure investment in access and aggregation produces less return.

## 5. Hidden Insights

- **The monetization gap is the most strategically dangerous gap.** Access and aggregation without monetization is infrastructure spending without payoff. Braddi flags this as her highest priority, which suggests leadership already knows the stakes.
- **The document implies upward pressure on execution pace.** The "quarter-by-quarter review" was requested by someone named Omid — a signal that senior leadership is asking for tighter visibility into progress. This is accountability being imposed from above, not volunteered from below.
- **Pricing is treated as a live, unresolved variable at two of three layers.** "AdX pricing" is called out as a major open component, and the document mentions a "detailed pricing review and refresh" was completed for the access pillar. Pricing strategy is being built in real time, not inherited from prior products.
- **The format of the follow-up email itself is a signal.** Braddi sends structured notes after the meeting, maps open questions to owners, and names the next milestone. This is how someone who understands accountability communicates upward — not to show off, but to make the gaps harder to ignore.
pullQuote: The smartest strategy documents don't just show where you're winning — they name exactly where the work isn't done yet.
leadershipTraits: Thinks in sequences, not just goals
Moves fast when the gap is named
